captions.instagram:
How does a printer work?

A heater boils ink into a bubble in three millionths of a second. A laser draws your page in static electricity. Open up an inkjet and a laser printer in 3D and watch every dot land.

→ Two ways to print: an inkjet squirts tiny drops, a laser printer melts powder onto the page.
→ A heater boils a skin of ink for 3 millionths of a second, and the bubble throws out a drop.
→ Row by row, thousands of drops a second spell out the page.
→ Only four inks and a yes-or-no dot, but at 600 dots per inch your eye sees every shade.
→ A laser draws the page as a pattern of charge on a spinning drum, and powder sticks to the pattern.

Play with it yourself. It's free and open source: glassbox-production-fd52.up.railway.app/printerclear (link in bio)

youtubeLong.title: How does a printer work? (interactive explainer)
youtubeLong.description:
A heater boils ink into a bubble in three millionths of a second. A laser draws your page in static electricity. Open up an inkjet and a laser printer in 3D and watch every dot land.

▶ Play with the interactive version: https://glassbox-production-fd52.up.railway.app/e/printerclear/
⌘ Source code (MIT): https://github.com/bdeeps/printerclear

In this video:
• Two machines, one job: dots. Every printer turns a page into millions of tiny dots.
• A bubble throws each drop. In a thermal inkjet, a 3 µs pulse heats a skin of ink to about 300 °C.
• Shades from yes-or-no dots. A printer can only print a dot or leave the paper white, so it makes shades by changing how many dots it prints, in neat rows (halftone) or scattered (dither).
• Charge, light, powder, heat. The laser printer's drum is charged to about −700 V.
• Pins, heat and plastic. Dot-matrix printers fire steel pins through an inked ribbon, which is why banks still use them for passbooks and carbon copies.
• The ink is the expensive part. Cartridge ink can cost over ₹1 lakh a litre because printers are often sold cheaply and paid for through ink.
